In the **Defender** portal, they are part of **Exposure Management**: Attack surface, Attack paths. This second experience offers an overview (paths over time, top five choke points, top five scenarios, main targets and entries), a filterable list (high, medium or low risk level, asset type, remediation status, period) and a **choke points** tab. By default, paths are sorted by risk level, which the risk engine calculates from the factors of each resource.
1vhedaif1t2: The map of a path highlights the **vulnerable nodes** (resources with security issues), the **entry points** (external access where an attack could begin), the **target assets** (critical resources aimed at) and the **choke points** (nodes where several paths converge). Hover over a node or a link to see how the path is built, then open the node to read the details. The **blast radius** feature of a choke point shows what the compromise of an asset could affect next. Paths can cross environments: a cloud VM, an identity, then an on-premises domain controller.
3vji1qpt0u: A choke point is generally better than an isolated node: a single fix breaks several paths. Between two links of the same path, prefer the one that is the cheapest and least risky to fix, for example removing an unnecessary network exposure before reworking an identity. 250d9ow7102: The remediation tab of a path groups the **recommendations** that fix the path and the **additional recommendations** that reduce the risk without fully fixing it. The Defender portal also tracks remediation progress and can correlate actions with incidents.

1a6a6qja5t8: The **cloud security explorer** queries the graph to proactively identify risks. You start from a **query template** or build a query by choosing a resource type, conditions (vulnerabilities, secrets, exposure, permissions) and relationships. Documented template examples: virtual machine with a plaintext secret able to authenticate to another machine, to a storage account or to a SQL database. Queries cover Azure, AWS and GCP. Like paths, the explorer requires Defender CSPM and its agentless components (and the Defender for Containers plan to query the container data layer).

cxviz3q4r9: Defender for Cloud assesses **Internet exposure** through two analyses: the **control plane configuration** (public IP addresses, load balancers) and **network reachability** (routing, security and firewall rules). A machine with no public address can still be exposed behind a load balancer. The resources assessed include virtual machines, virtual machine scale sets, databases (Azure SQL, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Cosmos DB, Synapse, RDS, GCP databases), storage (Azure, S3, GCS), AI services, containers (AKS, EKS, GKE) and API Management operations. The network components assessed include application gateways, load balancers, Azure Firewall, network security groups and subnets, as well as AWS and GCP load balancers.

bj9ldet5yy: In Defender for Cloud, a **compliance standard** relies on an Azure Policy initiative (or, for AWS and GCP, on the connector's assessments). The **regulatory compliance** dashboard shows the **Microsoft cloud security benchmark** (MCSB) by default. To track another standard (for example a payment card industry standard or an information security management standard), it must be added explicitly. It is the same mechanism as in module 5: without relevant assessed resources, an assigned standard **does not appear** on the dashboard, which often surprises people.
z9x8uhj5pz: To access additional standards, you must have enabled **at least one paid plan**, except Defender for Servers plan 1 and Defender for API plan 1: for Servers, compliance is offered only by plan 2. To add a standard, the **Owner** or **Policy Contributor** role is required. To **read** the data, the **Reader** role gives access to Azure Policy compliance data, which **Security Reader** does not. The documented minimum to access the dashboard and manage standards is the combination of **Resource Policy Contributor** and **Security Admin**.
ranxbuyk5m: In the Azure portal, Regulatory compliance then **Manage compliance policies**, you choose an account (subscription or management group, AWS account or management account, GCP project or organization), then Security policies where you toggle the standard to “On.” The documentation recommends **the highest applicable scope** so that data is aggregated for all nested resources. For AWS, the **AWS Foundational Security Best Practices** standard is assigned by default to each account. Others are added through Environment settings, the account, Standards, Add, Standard.
22dt3a6pble: The **Defender** portal offers consumption-oriented tracking (compliance indicator, filtering of recommendations by framework), but the **assignment** and configuration of standards remain in the **Azure** portal. A team that has access only to the Defender portal therefore cannot add a standard. Say so when defining roles (module 3).

1vdzj0401gk: A standard includes **controls**, logical groups of related recommendations. Defender for Cloud continuously assesses what can be assessed automatically and displays compliant or non-compliant resources. For each control, the **Control details** offer three tabs: **Overview**, **Your Actions** (your organization's actions, automated and manual) and **Microsoft Actions** (what Microsoft did to meet the standard in its share of responsibility). Automated assessments show the number of resources and resource types that fail and lead to remediation.
2bvr2tlrv9u: A grayed-out control has **no associated Defender for Cloud assessment**. Three reasons: the control concerns a procedure or process that a tool cannot verify; the automated assessment does not exist yet; or the control falls under the platform's responsibility. A grayed-out control is **neither compliant nor non-compliant**: it is not assessed. A report that counts grayed-out controls as compliant is misleading. The “shared responsibility” view is specific to Azure.
212r7czm9bo: For manual assessments, open the control, the **Manual attestation and evidence** section, select the assessment and the subscriptions concerned, then **Attest**. You enter the information and attach the **evidence** (document, link, capture). The attestation is a person's declaration, not a technical verification: it must name the author, the date, the scope and the evidence, and will be reexamined at a decided frequency. A free field filled with “OK” supports no audit.
19ejygaa62b: Assessments run about **every 12 hours**: the effect of a fix appears after the next run. On large scopes, Azure Policy evaluation has no guaranteed delay. To exclude a resource from an MCSB recommendation counted in the secure score, you create an **exemption** in the portal; for other recommendations, you create the exemption in Azure Policy. Each exemption must have a reason, an owner and an expiration.

1qa3dvavcm2: A Defender for Cloud recommendation describes a gap between the state of a resource and a standard, with the affected resources, the severity and the fix steps. In the Azure portal, **Recommendations**, then the **Take action** tab, you find four levers: **Remediate** (manual steps, and for some recommendations a **Fix** button with **View remediation logic** to read the logic before applying it), **Recommendation owner and set due date** (if a governance rule is enabled), **Exempt** (exemption) and **Workflow automation** (logic app triggered by the recommendation). The **Graph** tab shows the context used for risk prioritization, including attack paths.
237pwtna9u9: By default, recommendations are ordered by **risk level**. To this are added the Microsoft cloud security benchmark controls that influence the secure score. With the new format of **individual recommendations**, governance applies at the finding level, and recommendations marked **Preview** do not affect the risk-based secure score before general availability. A reasonable prioritization therefore crosses exposure, data sensitivity, attack path and effort, rather than the number of resources alone.
1096vi258oc: The **Fix** button exists only for certain recommendations: without it, you follow the manual steps. It fixes several resources at once, which is both an advantage and a risk: read the logic before applying. For AWS and GCP, an **automated remediation script** (CLI language) is generated, which you copy and run yourself. After the fix, the state update may take several minutes, and the full reassessment longer. An integration with **Security Copilot** (Summarize with Copilot, Fix with Copilot) exists, but it requires Security Copilot and security compute units; it does not replace human review.
kr2f50fdag: The documentation aimed at small organizations proposes a sequence that can be adopted as is: record the initial setting and the rollback method, apply the fix outside production, test the application, deployment and administrative access, then go through the change process for production. The required permissions are those of the operation on the resource: **Security Reader is not enough** to fix. A recommendation may remain visible until reassessment; do not repeat a disruptive change just because the state has not yet changed.
